reflection: light bouncing off a surface
refraction: light bending as it passes into water or glass
prism: a wedge of glass that splits white light into colours
absorb: to soak up light instead of bouncing it back
lens: a curved piece of glass that bends light
rainbow: sunlight split into colours by raindrops

When you flick a switch, the room fills with light at once, with no waiting. That is because light is the fastest thing in the whole universe. Nothing can travel quicker. In a single second, a beam of light could race around the entire Earth more than seven times. It is almost too fast to imagine.

image.note: A beam of light streaking round the globe seven times, drawn as a glowing loop; speed

pages.text: Most of our light comes from one place: the Sun. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to cross the vast gap of space and reach us. So the light warming your face right now actually left the Sun eight minutes ago. You are always seeing the Sun a little bit in the past.

image.note: The Sun with a beam labelled travelling to Earth; a clock showing eight minutes; clear diagram

pages.text: Here is a question most people get wrong. How do your eyes see a chair? Not by sending anything out. Light from the Sun or a lamp lands on the chair, bounces off it, and travels into your eyes. Your eyes catch that light, and your brain turns it into a picture. In a dark room with no light at all, even the sharpest eyes see nothing.

image.note: A diagram: lamp to chair to eye, arrows showing light bouncing off and entering the eye; simple

pages.text: This is why you cannot see in the dark, no matter how hard you stare. There is simply no light for your eyes to catch. Cats and owls seem to see at night, but even they need a tiny bit of light. Seeing is not something your eyes do to the world. It is something light does for your eyes.

image.note: A pitch-dark room, only a pair of puzzled eyes; then the same room with a lamp on, full of things

pages.text: Light usually travels in dead straight lines. That is why you get sharp shadows: the light cannot bend round the corner of an object, so a dark shape is left behind it. But light can be made to change direction. When it bounces off a smooth surface, we call that reflection. A mirror is simply a surface that bounces light back very cleanly.

image.note: A child making a hand shadow on a wall; beside it, light bouncing off a mirror at a neat angle

pages.text: Light can also bend. When a beam passes from air into water or glass, it slows and bends at the join. This is called refraction. It is why a straw in a glass of water looks broken at the surface, and why you can never quite grab a fish where it appears to be. The light lied to you, just a little.

image.note: A straw in a glass of water looking bent at the waterline; a puzzled child; gentle humour

pages.text: Now for the best secret of all. The light from the Sun looks white, or almost colourless. But it is hiding something. Long ago, a scientist let a beam of white light pass through a wedge of glass called a prism, and out of the other side spilled every colour of the rainbow. The white light had been carrying them all along.

image.note: A prism splitting a white beam into a fan of rainbow colours on a wall; wonder

pages.text: That is exactly what a rainbow is. When sunlight passes through millions of tiny raindrops after a shower, each drop acts like a little prism, splitting the light. The hidden colours spread out across the sky in a great arc. A rainbow is not painted on the sky. It is white sunlight, taken apart by rain.

image.note: A rainbow over a wet estate after rain, sun behind the viewer; a child pointing, delighted

pages.text: So why is a leaf green, or a mango yellow? Here is the surprise: the colour is not really in the object at all. White light, full of every colour, lands on the leaf. The leaf soaks up most of the colours but bounces the green light back to your eyes. You see green because green is the colour the leaf did not keep.

image.note: A green leaf with white light arriving and only green light bouncing to the eye; the rest absorbed

pages.text: A red cloth bounces back red and keeps the rest. A white shirt bounces back nearly everything, which is why it looks bright and stays cooler in the sun. A black car keeps almost all the light and turns it to heat, which is why it grows so hot to touch. Colour and heat, it turns out, are close cousins.

image.note: A white shirt and a black car in bright sun, heat rising off the dark car; everyday and clear

pages.text: Once people understood light, they learned to bend it on purpose. A curved lens in a pair of glasses bends light so a blurry world turns sharp. Two lenses in a telescope gather faint starlight and pull distant worlds close. The same trick lets a doctor see tiny germs through a microscope. Bending light is a kind of power.

image.note: Split image: spectacles sharpening a page, a telescope on stars, a microscope on a droplet

pages.text: The cleverest trick of all is trapping light inside thin strands of glass thinner than a hair. Light races along inside them, bouncing as it goes, carrying messages of every video call and message across cities and under oceans. When you watch a video on a screen, light itself is doing the carrying.

image.note: A glowing fibre-optic strand carrying pulses of light, branching out to phones and screens

pages.text: Stop and notice, then, how much of your world is really light doing its quiet work. Every colour you love, every face you know, every book you read, reaches you only because light bounced off it and into your eyes. You have been swimming in light your whole life without once thinking about it.

image.note: A busy, colourful Nigerian street market in bright sun, everything vivid; light everywhere

pages.text: So the next time a rainbow appears, or the sun warms your back, or a lamp pushes the dark out of a room, you will know the secret. Light is fast, it bounces and bends, it hides every colour, and it is the reason you can see anything at all. It is one of the great wonders, and it is switched on right in front of you.

image.note: A child by a sunny window, rainbow light from a prism scattered across their smiling face; closing, warm
